steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $11,200 from web design (3 clients). Interest $2,340 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Interactive Brokers). Home office: 110 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,250 (Sallie Mae, 2017–2020); charity $1,100 to Local United Way with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $950. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s a clear plan for your 2024 federal return (married filing jointly, Seattle WA).

Key deductions and which to take
- Standard vs itemized
  - Itemized you mentioned: $1,100 cash charity to United Way (with receipt).
  - Unreimbursed employee expenses ($950) are not deductible for most W-2 employees in 2018–2025 unless you’re a reservist, qualified performing artist, fee-basis government official, or have impairment-related expenses.
  - You don’t have mortgage interest or state income tax (WA), and sales tax/property tax weren’t provided.
  - 2024 standard deduction (MFJ): $29,200. This is far larger than your likely itemized deductions, so take the standard deduction.

- Student loan interest
  - You paid $4,250, but the above-the-line deduction is capped at $2,500. Your income is low enough to get the full $2,500. Report on Schedule 1; you’ll typically need Form 1098-E.

Home office for your web design business (Schedule C)
- Eligibility reminder: space must be used regularly and exclusively for the business and be your principal place for admin/management or client meetings.
- Facts: office 110 sq ft, apartment 680 sq ft → business-use percentage ≈ 110/680 = 16.2%. Annual rent = $1,600 x 12 = $19,200.

Two methods:
1) Simplified method
   - Deduction = $5 x 110 sq ft = $550. No Form 8829 required (just use the Schedule C line for simplified method).

2) Actual-expense method (requires Form 8829)
   - Deductible indirect rent = $19,200 x 16.2% ≈ $3,108.
   - This is much larger than the simplified amount. If you also had utilities, renters insurance, internet, etc., the actual method would be even more favorable. Keep records.

Which method is better here?
- Actual-expense method saves you roughly $1,900 of taxable income compared with the simplified method (details below), so I recommend actual + Form 8829 if you meet the home-office rules and are comfortable with the recordkeeping.

Estimated numbers to show the difference
- Schedule C net profit
  - Simplified: $11,200 − $550 = $10,650
  - Actual: $11,200 − $3,108 ≈ $8,092

- Self-employment (SE) tax and deduction
  - Simplified: SE tax ≈ $1,504; deductible half ≈ $752
  - Actual: SE tax ≈ $1,143; deductible half ≈ $571

- Adjusted gross income (AGI)
  - Simplified: 82,350 (W-2) + 10,650 (Sch C) + 2,340 (interest) + 440 (dividends) − 2,500 (student loan interest) − 752 (½ SE tax) ≈ $92,528
  - Actual: 82,350 + 8,092 + 2,340 + 440 − 2,500 − 571 ≈ $90,151

- Taxable income before QBI (199A)
  - Simplified: $92,528 − $29,200 = $63,328
  - Actual: $90,151 − $29,200 = $60,951

- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (Form 8995)
  - QBI base is your business profit reduced by the deductible half of SE tax.
  - Simplified: (10,650 − 752) x 20% ≈ $1,980
  - Actual: (8,092 − 571) x 20% ≈ $1,504

- Taxable income after QBI
  - Simplified: $63,328 − $1,980 ≈ $61,348
  - Actual: $60,951 − $1,504 ≈ $59,447
  - Actual-expense method lowers taxable income by about $1,901 vs. simplified.

Which forms you’ll use
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1: student loan interest deduction; also where your Schedule C/SE amounts flow to 1040
- Schedule B: your interest and dividends exceed $1,500, so list the $2,340 (Chase) and $440 (Interactive Brokers)
- Schedule C: report the $11,200 web design income and expenses
- Schedule SE: compute self-employment tax
- Form 8829: for home office using the actual-expense method (not needed if using the simplified method)
- Form 8995: Qualified Business Income deduction (likely the simple version, given your income)
- Schedule A: only if you decide to itemize (not recommended based on current info)

Other notes and tips
- Charity: You have the receipt, which is required for a cash gift > $250. You’ll only use it if you itemize.
- Dividends: Check your 1099-DIV to see how much is qualified vs. ordinary; that can slightly affect your tax rate on the dividends line.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses: Generally not deductible for W-2 employees through 2025. If any of the $950 was actually for your web design business, it may belong on Schedule C instead—let me know.
- Washington: No state income tax return. If your business is in WA, you may have state B&O/SE tax or city business licensing/filing requirements—separate from the federal return.
- Quarterly estimates for future years: With self-employment income, consider making quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) to avoid underpayment penalties.

If you confirm the home office meets the exclusive/regular use test and that you don’t have additional business expenses (utilities, internet, software, equipment, subscriptions, domain/hosting, payment processing fees), I can finalize the actual-expense method numbers and produce a tidy checklist of entries for each form.
